adult ventricular myocytes cultured in medium 199 for 6 days retain their rod shape and striated structure, but lose 57% of their transverse tubules and 50-65% of their L-type Ca and inwardly rectifying K channels.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the preservation and/or alteration of cellular and molecular properties in myocytes maintained for extended periods in vitro.
the effects of cell culture on the morphology, electrophysiological properties, and gene expression of adult rabbit ventricular cells.
the effects of culture conditions on the electrophysiology and morphology of isolated rabbit ventricular myocyte.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the changes in morphology and ion channel density in adult rabbit myocytes in cell culture over 6 days are not consistent with a simple model of cell deterioration, but may reflect a complex process of cell adaptation.

the adult rabbit ventricular cell is a useful model for cardiac electrophysiology, but that caution should be used when interpreting data obtained from myocytes cultured for more than 24 h, especially in terms of ion channel density.

the cultured myocytes are not the same as freshly isolated ones, but they do retain some of the characteristics of the intact tissue, and may be a valuable model for the study of cardiac electrophysiology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the adult rabbit ventricular cell is a useful model for studying cardiac ion channels but that care must be taken to ensure that cells are studied in their optimal state, i.e. within the first day of isolation.
the adult ventricular myocyte is not a static entity but rather a dynamic structure whose properties change in a time- and cell-type-dependent fashion.
myocytes in culture are a useful model for some aspects of cardiac physiology, but that they are not an ideal model for others.
The main takeaway from our work is that
myocytes in culture may not be an ideal preparation for studying the molecular basis of arrhythmia.
ion channel currents in cultured myocytes are not a good reflection of their density in the intact heart.

the time course for changes in ion channel density and transverse tubules density in culture may be quite rapid and that this should be considered in the design and interpretation of experiments using cultured cardiac myocytes.
